tip: Question word + και να (ke na) = '-ever': όπως και να το δεις (ópos ke na to dhis) = however you look at it. Same pattern: ό,τι και να (óti ke na) = whatever.
The -οντας (-ondas) ending works like English '-ing': συνοψίζοντας (sinopsízondas) = summing up. One word does the job of English 'to sum up'.
Στο κάτω κάτω (sto káto káto) is literally 'at the bottom bottom' – the doubled κάτω (káto) is one Greek way of saying 'at the end of the day'.
Θα έπρεπε (tha éprepe) = should, ought to – θα (tha) in front of the past form of πρέπει (prépi = must) turns it into advice.
Φταίω (ftéo) = to be at fault: εγώ φταίω (eghó ftéo) = it's my fault; φταίνε (fténe) = they are at fault.
Greek's 'as ... as' is τόσο ... όσο (tóso ... óso): τόσο απλό όσο ακούγεται (tóso apló óso akúyete) = as simple as it sounds.
Conclusions aren't drawn in Greek – they're taken out: βγάλουμε συμπεράσματα (vghálume simberásmata), from βγάζω (vgházo = take out).
Put καλο- (kalo = well) in front of a verb and it usually means doing it thoroughly: καλοσκεφτείς (kaloskeftís) = think it over, not just σκεφτείς (skeftís = think).
Έχει λογική (ékhi loyikí) = it makes sense, literally 'it has logic'. Greek has the sense rather than making it.
Εν τέλει (en téli) is the Greek 'in the end'; the word-for-word στο τέλος της ημέρας (sto télos tis iméras) sounds like translated English.
Greek stacks negatives where English avoids them: ούτε υπέρ ούτε κατά (úte ipér úte katá = neither for nor against) still normally needs δεν (dhen) before the verb.
Αν και (an ke) looks like 'if and' but means 'even though': αν και διαφωνούμε (an ke dhiafonúme) = even though we disagree. The verb keeps its normal form.
Παρακαλείσθε όπως (parakalísthe ópos) is the fixed official formula for 'you are requested to' – you'll meet it in notices and letters, hardly ever in speech.
Διά της παρούσης (dhia tis parúsis = by the present letter) is the fixed 'hereby' opener of official documents, formal wording kept from the older written language.
Εκδημία (ekdhimía) is the formal word for death in announcements, literally a 'departure from home'. Everyday Greek says θάνατος (thánatos).
Συμβάσεως (simváseos = of the contract) uses the formal -εως (-eos) of-form; everyday Greek says σύμβασης (símvasis). Contracts and official letters keep the old ending.
Formal invitations say εσπέρα (espéra) for evening; everyday Greek says βράδυ (vrádhi). Wedding and baptism cards run on this elevated style.
Τυγχάνει επεξεργασίας (tinkháni epexerghasías = is being processed) is officialese, literally 'it chances upon processing', the formal way to say 'it is being handled'.
Δύνανται (dhínande) is legal-formal for 'they may' – everyday Greek says μπορούν (borún). Regulations and notices keep the old verb.
Θυγατρός (thighatrós = of the daughter) is the old formal of-form; everyday Greek says της κόρης (tis kóris). Birth announcements keep it.
Άμα τη δύσει (áma ti dhísi) is a fossil: literally 'at the setting', old grammar surviving on signs. Everyday Greek says στη δύση του ήλιου (sti dhísi tu ilíu).
Αμελλητί (amelití) is legalese for 'without delay' in a single word; everyday Greek uses the phrase χωρίς καθυστέρηση (khorís kathistérisi).
Μεσημβρία (mesimvría) is the formal word for noon – hotel notices use it where everyday Greek says μεσημέρι (mesiméri).
Ουδείς (udhís) is the formal 'no one' of rules and regulations – everyday Greek says κανείς (kanís). Seeing it usually signals officialese.
Απηύθυνε (apífthine = addressed) is the formal past; everyday Greek says απεύθυνε (apéfthine). The formal form swaps the ε (e) for η (i) at the start.
Εβαπτίσθη (evaptísthi = was baptized) is the formal was-done form; everyday Greek says βαφτίστηκε (vaftístike). Church and official notices keep the -θη (-thi) ending.
Απεκόπη (apekópi = was cut off) is the short formal was-done form; everyday speech says αποκόπηκε (apokópike). Essays on art and history favor the old ending.
Ευρίσκεται (evrískete) is the formal face of everyday βρίσκεται (vrískete = is located) – the older ευ- (ev-) beginning survives in brochures and listings.
Ευχόμεθα (efkhómetha = we wish) keeps the old -μεθα (-metha) 'we' ending; everyday Greek says ευχόμαστε (efkhómaste). Formal wishes run on this ending.
Proverb on haste: όποιος βιάζεται σκοντάφτει (ópios viázete skondáfti = whoever hurries stumbles).
